title: “FOR I KNOW THE PLANS I HAVE FOR YOU” — JEREMIAH 29:11 IS NOT SAYING WHAT MANY CHRISTIANS THINK
paragraphs: “FOR I KNOW THE PLANS I HAVE FOR YOU” — JEREMIAH 29:11 IS NOT SAYING WHAT MANY CHRISTIANS THINK

We turned one of Scripture’s most painful promises into a slogan about getting the life we wanted. But when you put Jeremiah 29:11 back into Babylon, the verse becomes harder, deeper—and far more beautiful.
You have probably seen it on a graduation card.
Printed beneath a sunrise.
Framed above a desk.
Posted after someone got the job.
Quoted when the relationship finally worked out.
Whispered when somebody desperately needed to believe that the next chapter of life would be better than the last.
“For I know the plans I have for you…”
And somewhere along the way, many of us began hearing something God never actually said.
You are going to get the future you imagined.
This disappointment will disappear soon.
Your career will work out.
Your dream will happen.
The person will come back.
The diagnosis will change.
The door will open.
The money will arrive.
Everything is about to fall into place.
But what if I told you Jeremiah 29:11 was originally spoken to people whose lives had already fallen apart?
Not people standing at the doorway of their dream.
Exiles.
People who had lost their homeland.
People living under the shadow of Babylon.
People who wanted to go home.
And God essentially told them:
Not yet.
That changes the verse.
And perhaps it needs to change the way some of us understand God.
Because the Bible does not become less comforting when we read it correctly.
It becomes more comforting.
The Hebrew of Jeremiah 29:11 reads:
כִּי אָנֹכִי יָדַעְתִּי אֶת־הַמַּחֲשָׁבֹת אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי חֹשֵׁב עֲלֵיכֶם נְאֻם־יְהוָה מַחְשְׁבוֹת שָׁלוֹם וְלֹא לְרָעָה לָתֵת לָכֶם אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה
Ki anokhi yada'ti et-hamachashavot asher anokhi choshev aleikhem, ne'um-YHWH; machshevot shalom velo lera'ah, latet lakhem acharit vetikvah.
A careful sense of the verse is:
“For I know the plans—or intentions—I am planning concerning you,” declares the LORD, “plans of shalom and not of calamity, to give you a future and a hope.”
Notice that word.
Shalom.
שָׁלוֹם
We often reduce shalom to “peace,” but biblical shalom can carry the richer sense of welfare, wholeness, well-being, soundness, things being put right.
And that matters enormously.
God was not promising His exiled people immediate comfort.
He was declaring that catastrophe would not have the final word over His covenant purposes.
There would be an acharit—אַחֲרִית—a future, an outcome, an end beyond what they could presently see.
There would be tikvah—תִּקְוָה—hope.
But here is the detail that rarely makes it onto the coffee mug.
One verse earlier, God tells them how long Babylon will last.
Seventy years.
Read that slowly.
Seventy.
Years.

The people receiving Jeremiah’s letter were being warned against false hopes of an immediate escape. God told the exiles to build houses and live in them. Plant gardens. Eat their produce. Marry. Have children. Multiply. Seek the shalom of the city where they had been carried into exile. Pray for it.
In other words:
You are going to be here for a while.
Imagine receiving that message when you had been praying every night to leave.
Imagine begging God to open the prison door…
and God telling you to plant a garden outside it.
Imagine asking God when your old life is coming back…
and hearing Him tell you to become faithful in the life you never wanted.
That is Jeremiah 29:11.
And suddenly the verse stops sounding like motivational Christianity.
It starts sounding like something strong enough to keep a human soul alive when God does not remove Babylon.
Maybe that is why this verse needs to be rescued from the way we sometimes use it.
Because somebody reading this is living in a Babylon you never chose.
You prayed.
Nothing moved.
You believed.
The door stayed closed.
You tried to remain faithful, but the marriage still fractured.
You asked God for healing, but you are still waiting.
You raised the child in church, and now you barely recognize the person they have become.
You thought obedience would produce a straight road.
Instead, obedience led you into a wilderness.
You watched other people testify about answered prayers while yours seemed to disappear into the ceiling.
And perhaps someone handed you Jeremiah 29:11 as though it meant:
“Don't worry. God is about to give you what you want.”
Then He didn't.
And somewhere inside you, something cracked.
Maybe you wondered whether God had forgotten His promise.
But what if the promise was even greater than what you thought?
God never promised Israel that Babylon was imaginary.
He promised Babylon would not be final.
There is a difference.
A massive one.
Biblical hope is not pretending the furnace is cold.
Biblical hope is discovering that God remains God inside the fire.
It is not believing Christians will never enter valleys.
It is knowing the Shepherd enters valleys with His sheep.
It is not believing every earthly story receives the ending we request.
It is trusting that no earthly chapter can overthrow the redemptive purposes of God.
And Jeremiah's message gets even more uncomfortable.
Before the promise comes a warning.
False prophets were telling the people what they wanted to hear.
God warned the exiles not to be deceived by them.
Think about that.
There were voices offering quick deliverance.
Jeremiah offered faithful endurance.
There were voices saying Babylon would soon disappear.
God said:
Build.
Plant.
Live.
Pray.
Wait.
And then came:
“I know the plans…”
Maybe some of us have unknowingly preferred the false prophet's version of Jeremiah 29:11.
The version where God exists to guarantee our timeline.
The version where faith means getting promoted.
The version where favor means becoming comfortable.
The version where suffering must mean something has gone wrong.
The version where God's plan is automatically identified with whatever future we happen to desire most.
But Scripture refuses to make God the servant of our dreams.
God is not writing our story merely to make us impressive.
He is drawing His people back to Himself.
And that becomes unmistakable when you keep reading.
Jeremiah 29 does not stop at verse 11.
God continues:
“You will call upon Me…”
“You will pray to Me…”
“You will seek Me…”
And then comes one of the most beautiful statements in the chapter:
וּבִקַּשְׁתֶּם אֹתִי וּמְצָאתֶם כִּי תִדְרְשֻׁנִי בְּכָל־לְבַבְכֶם
Uviqqashtem oti umetzatem, ki tidreshuni bekhol-levavkhem.
“You will seek Me and find Me when you seek Me with all your heart.”
There it is.
Maybe the greatest gift in Jeremiah 29 was never simply getting out of Babylon.
It was getting Israel's heart back toward God.
We want God's plans.
God wants our hearts.
We want the future.
God says:
Seek Me.
We want the breakthrough.
God says:
Call upon Me.
We want Babylon removed.
God says:
Do not waste Babylon.
There are things God can form in exile that comfort could never teach us.
Not because suffering is inherently good.
Not because tragedy should be romanticized.
Not because every painful event can casually be labeled “God's plan.”
Scripture never gives us permission to call evil good.
But Scripture repeatedly shows us a God so sovereign, wise, and redemptive that evil does not get the privilege of writing the final sentence.
And that brings us to Jesus.
Because Christians cannot read the story of exile, promise, restoration, hope, judgment, mercy, and homecoming without eventually seeing the entire biblical story rushing toward Christ.
Humanity has a deeper Babylon.
Sin.
We have not merely experienced brokenness.
We have participated in it.
We have lied.
Lusted.
Hated.
Envied.
Hidden.
Manipulated.
Worshiped ourselves.
Excused what God calls sin.
Built private idols while publicly appearing religious.
We have wanted God's blessings while resisting God's authority.
And no motivational interpretation of Jeremiah 29:11 can solve that problem.
We do not merely need better plans.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need redemption.
We need a Savior.
And Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve our earthly circumstances.
He came to rescue sinners.
The cross destroys the fantasy that God's love means the absence of suffering.
Look at Jesus.
The sinless Son of God betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
If suffering automatically meant God had abandoned His plan, Calvary would appear to be history's greatest failure.
Instead, Calvary became the center of redemption.
What looked like scandal became grace.
What looked like defeat became victory.
What looked like the end became the doorway to resurrection.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the nails never pierced Him.
By rising with the scars.
And maybe somebody needs that distinction tonight.
God's plan for you does not necessarily mean you will get everything you have been asking for.
It means that for those who belong to Christ, your suffering cannot cancel God's faithfulness.
Your disappointment cannot dethrone Jesus.
Your past cannot overpower the blood of Christ.
Your worst chapter does not possess authority over your final identity.
Your sin does not have to become your destiny if you turn to Christ in repentance and faith.
Your shame does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Maybe your marriage did not survive.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe the business failed.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe somebody walked away.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe your body was not healed when you begged for healing.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe you are rebuilding from consequences you caused yourself.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe you wasted years.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe you are reading this with tears nobody knows about.
Jesus is still Lord.
Christian hope is not:
“Everything I want will eventually happen.”
Christian hope is:
“Whatever happens, Christ will remain faithful, death will not have the last word, resurrection is real, and everyone who belongs to Jesus has a future no Babylon can steal.”
That is stronger than a slogan.
That can survive a funeral.
That can survive rejection.
That can survive bankruptcy.
That can survive betrayal.
That can survive unanswered questions.
That can survive the night when you cannot feel God at all.
Because Christian hope ultimately rests not in circumstances but in a Person.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where Jeremiah 29:11 becomes personal without becoming selfish.

The original “you” belongs in its historical setting. Jeremiah was writing God's word to the Judean exiles as a people. We should not rip that covenant promise from its context and pretend every detail was directly addressed to twenty-first-century individuals.
But the God revealed there is still the God Christians worship.
A God who keeps covenant.
A God who judges sin seriously.
A God who refuses to abandon His redemptive purposes.
A God who calls His people to seek Him wholeheartedly.
And the New Testament gives believers promises even greater than the shallow version we sometimes try to manufacture from Jeremiah 29:11.
In Christ, God does not promise that every circumstance will become pleasant.
He promises that nothing can separate His people from His love.
He does not promise exemption from tribulation.
Jesus explicitly told His disciples that they would have trouble in this world.
He does not promise Christians a life untouched by grief.
He promises resurrection.
He promises forgiveness through Christ.
He promises His presence.
He promises an inheritance that cannot be destroyed.
He promises that the story of everyone united to Jesus ends not in exile but home.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
“What plans does God have for my dream?”
Perhaps the question becomes:
“Jesus, what are You doing with my heart while I wait?”
That question is harder.
And holier.
Because maybe you have spent years asking God to change your surroundings while He has been exposing what lives inside you.
Pride.
Bitterness.
Unforgiveness.
Secret sin.
The addiction nobody knows about.
The relationship you know dishonors Him.
The resentment you keep feeding.
The version of Christianity that wants blessing without surrender.
What if your greatest danger is not that God's plan will fail?
What if your greatest danger is becoming so obsessed with escaping Babylon that you miss God's invitation to seek Him there?
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Maybe you do not need another inspirational quote tonight.
Maybe you need repentance.
Maybe you need to stop negotiating with the sin Jesus died to save you from.
Maybe you need to stop calling disobedience “a complicated season.”
Maybe you need to forgive.
Maybe you need to confess.
Maybe you need to come home.
Not to religion.
To Christ.
If that is you, do not hide behind Christian language.
Jesus already knows.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him your unbelief.
Bring Him the broken pieces.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people can improve themselves.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and that forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life are offered through Him.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
And if you are already His but exhausted from waiting, hear this carefully:
Your waiting is not proof that God has forgotten you.
Jeremiah's exiles had to learn that a delayed promise was not an abandoned promise.
Plant the garden.
Pray.
Stay faithful.
Seek God.
Love people.
Obey what Scripture has already made clear.
Stop demanding that God show you the entire map before you take the next faithful step.
And when tomorrow still looks like Babylon…
remember who holds tomorrow.
Pray for somebody.
Encourage somebody.
Remind somebody that Jesus has not finished writing their story.
Not because God needs our money.
Not because clicking a button proves our faith.
But because Christians have always used their time, resources, voices, generosity, and opportunities to help truthful ministry reach others.
If you genuinely want to glorify God through supporting this work, do it freely, prayerfully, and for Christ—not from guilt.
If you have been consuming truth quietly, perhaps today is the day to help carry it farther.
Follow.
But never confuse the ministry with the Messiah.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A church membership cannot save you.
Your generosity cannot save you.
Your morality cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
And perhaps that is the truth Jeremiah 29:11 has been trying to teach us beneath all our inspirational posters.
God's faithfulness is bigger than the future you planned.
Sometimes He does open the door.
Sometimes He makes us faithful while the door remains closed.
Sometimes He restores what was lost.
Sometimes He teaches us that Christ Himself is better than what we lost.
Sometimes He leads us home quickly.
Sometimes the road runs through Babylon.
But for those who belong to Jesus, Babylon never gets to write the ending.
So the next time you read:
“For I know the plans I have for you…”
do not hear:
“God owes me the life I imagined.”
Hear something stronger.
The God who sees the entire story has not surrendered His throne because you cannot understand this chapter.
The God who brought redemption through a cross can be trusted when your story looks nothing like the one you would have written.
And the Savior who walked out of a grave is still writing stories that graves, failures, scandals, sins, betrayals, disappointments, and exiles cannot finish.
You may be standing in a chapter you never would have chosen—but if Jesus holds the pen, Babylon does not get the final sentence.
